Reproducing Carrier et al. (2026) from Zenodo records 17624449 and 17794764¶

Paper. Carrier MA, Romano DM, Scaria A, Palmer H, O'Leary T, Marder E, Powell D (2026). The combined effects of temperature and salinity on the stomatogastric nervous system of two species of decapod crustacea. J Neurophysiol 135: 797-814. doi:10.1152/jn.00294.2025. The claims file (claims/carrier-2026.yaml) was written from the version of record (full text, Methods, figure legends, Table 1); the paper has no supplement.

Datasets. Two Zenodo records the authors deposited for the paper, both read at the only version each has (Zenodo pins a version by its record id; the paper cites these record DOIs, and the target list gives no other version):

  • ZENODO:17624449 (Part I, folder zenodo-17624449), record 17624449, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.17624449, published 2025-11-16.
  • ZENODO:17794764 (Part II, folder zenodo-17794764), record 17794764, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.17794764, published 2025-12-02.

Files read, with the MD5 each record lists (checked when a file is read whole; members of the large zips are read in place):

What is tested on what. The isolated-STNS claims are tested on the authors' own per-preparation values in the deposited analysis tables (PD burst frequency of the final 30 s of each step, crash steps and crash temperatures, phases). The raw recordings (Spike2 for lobster, ABF for crab; about 51 GB of zips, read here at about 1 MB/s per connection) are listed but their burst detection is not repeated: the paper does not give its burst criteria, and the tables are the paper's own reading of the recordings. The in vivo PPG recordings are analysed from the raw .abf files.

import io
import time
import warnings

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from scipy import stats

import stns

pd.set_option("display.width", 220)
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 40)
pd.set_option("display.max_rows", 300)
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
started = time.time()

files1, files2 = stns.file_list(stns.PART1), stns.file_list(stns.PART2)
for rec, fl in ((stns.PART1, files1), (stns.PART2, files2)):
    print(f"Record {rec}: {len(fl)} files, {sum(v['size'] for v in fl.values()) / 1e9:.2f} GB")
    for k, v in sorted(fl.items()):
        print(f"  {v['size'] / 1e6:12.3f} MB  {v['md5']}  {k}")

raw = {k: stns.read_file(stns.PART1, k) for k in [
    "Crab Metadata.xlsx", "Lobster Pyloric Frequencies.xlsx", "CanboVsHomam_freqQ10s_1x.prism",
    "CanboVsHomam_CrashTemps.prism", "Phase Slopes.prism", "Crab & Lobster Nonlin fit of 1x.csv",
    "Crab & Lobster Nonlin fit of 075x.csv", "Crab & Lobster Nonlin fit of 125x.csv"]}
crab_x = pd.read_excel(io.BytesIO(raw["Crab Metadata.xlsx"]), sheet_name=None, header=None)
lob_x = pd.read_excel(io.BytesIO(raw["Lobster Pyloric Frequencies.xlsx"]), sheet_name=None, header=None)
pr_freq = stns.prism_data(raw["CanboVsHomam_freqQ10s_1x.prism"])
pr_crash = stns.prism_data(raw["CanboVsHomam_CrashTemps.prism"])
pr_phase = stns.prism_data(raw["Phase Slopes.prism"])
print("\nAll eight small files read whole; MD5 checked against the record's list.")

What the files hold¶

Every sheet of the two workbooks and every data sheet of the three Prism files, with its shape. The Prism files are zip archives (Prism 10 format) of JSON and CSV; their data tables are read from the CSV.

# Members of the large zips: names and sizes from the central directories (read in place).
f, zl = stns.open_zip(stns.PART1, "Lobster STNS.zip")
lob_members = pd.DataFrame([{"name": i.filename, "size": i.file_size, "crc": i.CRC} for i in zl.infolist()])
lob_members["ext"] = lob_members.name.str.extract(r"\.([A-Za-z0-9]+)$")[0].str.lower()
lob_members["prep"] = lob_members.name.str.split("/").str[1]
print("Lobster STNS.zip:", len(lob_members), "members; by extension:")
print(lob_members.ext.value_counts(dropna=False).to_string())
print("Preparation folders:", sorted(lob_members.prep.dropna().unique()[lob_members.prep.dropna().unique() != ""]))
rec_files = lob_members[lob_members.ext.isin(["smr", "smrx"])]
print("\nSpike2 recordings (top level of each folder, not the per-step copies under 'For Analysis'):")
top = rec_files[~rec_files.name.str.contains("For Analysis")]
print(top[["name", "size"]].to_string(index=False))
same = rec_files[rec_files.duplicated(["size", "crc"], keep=False)].sort_values(["size", "crc"])
print("\nSpike2 recordings with the same size and CRC-32 as another:", len(same))
print(same[["name", "size"]].to_string(index=False) if len(same) else "")
nested = {}
for rec, key in ((stns.PART1, "Raw Crab Data 1.zip"), (stns.PART2, "Raw Crab Data 2.zip"),
                 (stns.PART2, "Crab In Vivo Data 1.zip"), (stns.PART2, "Crab In Vivo Data 2.zip"),
                 (stns.PART2, "Lobster In Vivo Data 1.zip"), (stns.PART2, "Lobster In Vivo Data 2.zip")):
    fh, z = stns.open_zip(rec, key)
    nested[key] = [(i.filename, i.file_size) for i in z.infolist() if not i.filename.endswith("/")]
    fh.close()
    print(f"\n{key}: {len(nested[key])} members, {sum(s for _, s in nested[key]) / 1e9:.2f} GB uncompressed")
    for n, s in nested[key]:
        print(f"  {s / 1e6:10.1f} MB  {n}")

# What else the deposit holds, for the claims blocked on missing data (fig1e, fig4, fig5b).
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

import scipy.io as sio

print("Lobster STNS.zip, the 14 Excel files:")
print("\n".join("  " + n for n in lob_members[lob_members.ext == "xlsx"].name))
txt = lob_members[lob_members.ext == "txt"].copy()
txt["pattern"] = txt.name.str.split("/").str[-1].str.replace(r"\d+(\.\d+)?", "#", regex=True)
print("\nLobster STNS.zip, the", len(txt), "text files by name pattern (#: a number, such as a temperature):")
print(txt.groupby("pattern").agg(files=("name", "size"), folders=("prep", "nunique"),
                                 example=("name", "first")).sort_values("files", ascending=False).to_string())

print("\nFirst entries of each of the 21 inner Raw Crab zips (first 8 MB decompressed):")
inner = [(stns.PART1, "Raw Crab Data 1.zip", n) for n, _ in nested["Raw Crab Data 1.zip"]] + \
        [(stns.PART2, "Raw Crab Data 2.zip", n) for n, _ in nested["Raw Crab Data 2.zip"]]
t0 = time.time()
with ThreadPoolExecutor(4) as ex:
    heads = list(ex.map(lambda j: stns.member_head_names(*j), inner))
dt = time.time() - t0
print(f"  ({len(inner)} x 8 MB in {dt:.0f} s with 4 threads: {len(inner) * 8 / dt:.1f} MB/s in all, "
      f"{len(inner) * 8 / dt / 4:.1f} MB/s per inner zip)")
for (_, _, n), h in zip(inner, heads):
    print(f"  {n.split('/')[-1]}: {h[:3]}")

mats = {k: sio.loadmat(io.BytesIO(stns.read_file(stns.PART1, k))) for k in
        ["Crab_Q10s_1x&075x.mat", "Crab_Q10s_1x&125x.mat", "Lobster_Q10s_1x&075x.mat", "Lobster_Q10s_1x&125x.mat"]}
print("\nVariables of the four MATLAB files (MD5 checked):")
for k, m in mats.items():
    print(f"  {k}: " + ", ".join(f"{v} {m[v].shape}" for v in m if not v.startswith("__")))

s1 = lob_x["1x saline"]
print("\nLobster workbook, sheet '1x saline': header row", s1.iloc[0, 1:15].tolist())
print("  column 0 (row labels):", s1.iloc[:, 0].tolist())
v = s1[pd.to_numeric(s1[0], errors="coerce").between(10, 34)].iloc[:, 1:].apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").stack()
print(f"  values in the temperature rows: {v.min():.3f} to {v.max():.3f}")
ps = crab_x["Phase (Salinity)"]
print("\nCrab workbook, sheet 'Phase (Salinity)': header row", ps.iloc[0].tolist())
print("  column 0 (row labels):", ps.iloc[:, 0].tolist())

The raw crab data are 21 zips inside the two Raw Crab Data zips (Google Drive export parts, each 1.1 to 2.1 GB, deflated inside the outer zip). Each holds one zip per preparation, of ABF files named by preparation (or date) and sequence number only (888_144_0052.abf), with no salinity, step or protocol in the name; listing a whole part means decompressing all of it, about 37 GB in all, at the rate printed above for one stream, so only the first entries of each part are read. They show that the parts hold the crab salinity-series preparations (888_144, 888_139, 888_138 and 888_143 open four of them) as well as the ramp preparations.

The lobster folder holds the temperature ramps only: the Excel and text files are burst tables per preparation, ramp and step (1x, 0.75x and 1.25x), with LP and PY burst files in eight preparations' folders (counted below, under "Blocked claims"). There are no lobster salinity-series recordings or tables (Fig. 4), and no folder for preparation 888_156, which the lobster frequency table includes. The lobster workbook's 1x saline sheet holds 1x ramp frequencies (10 to 28 C), and the crab Phase (Salinity) sheet holds crab salinity-series phases; neither holds a lobster neuron crash temperature. The four MATLAB files hold the frequencies of the four Q10 comparisons (norm, low, high, one column per preparation, one row per step) and values derived from them.

Data check¶

The tables are put into tidy form. Each check of the tables against what the paper and the file names say is stated under its output. The tables hold one value per preparation and step (or salinity) and carry no time stamps, so there is no clock to align; the in vivo recordings' own start times are checked in their section.

Units are not stated in the tables; the values (crab 0.7 to 4.9, lobster 0.1 to 2.8 except one value, see below) are burst frequencies in Hz, the paper's unit, and temperatures in C on the paper's 2 C steps from 10 C. The crab sets hold 11 preparations (0.75x set) and 10 (1.25x set), as the paper's 11 (Fig. 2B) and 10 (Fig. 7C).

In [6]:
# The Prism data the paper's Q10 fits used are the Excel values: match each Prism column to a
# preparation by its values.
def match_columns(wide, tidy, sal, lo=10, hi=30):
    rows = []
    for c in wide.columns:
        v = wide[c].loc[lo:hi]
        if v.notna().sum() == 0:
            continue
        best = []
        for p, g in tidy[tidy.salinity == sal].groupby("prep"):
            s = g.drop_duplicates("temp").set_index("temp").freq.reindex(v.index)
            both = v.notna() & s.notna()
            if both.sum() and np.allclose(v[both], s[both], atol=1e-5) and both.sum() == v.notna().sum():
                best.append(p)
        rows.append({"prism_column": c, "points": int(v.notna().sum()), "matches": best})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

links = {}
for sal, key in ((1.0, "1x"), (0.75, "0.75x"), (1.25, "1.25x")):
    g = stns.prism_xy_groups(pr_freq[key])
    for title, w in g.items():
        tidy = crab_f if title.startswith("Canbo") else lob_f
        m = match_columns(w, tidy, sal)
        links[title] = m
        n_one = (m.matches.str.len() == 1).sum()
        print(f"{title}: {len(m)} columns with data; matched to exactly one preparation: {n_one}; "
              f"to several: {(m.matches.str.len() > 1).sum()}; to none: {(m.matches.str.len() == 0).sum()}")
        for _, r in m[m.matches.str.len() != 1].iterrows():
            print(f"    column {r.prism_column} ({r.points} points) matches {r.matches}")
print("\nLobster preparations in Sheet4 but in no Prism column:")
for sal, key in ((1.0, "Homam 1x"), (0.75, "Homam 0.75x"), (1.25, "Homam 1.25x")):
    used = {p for ps in links[key].matches for p in ps}
    print(f"  {sal}x:", sorted(set(lob_f[lob_f.salinity == sal].prep) - used))

Every Prism column of the frequency file is a preparation of the Excel tables, value for value. One lobster 0.75x column matches two preparations, 111122 and 120722: their 0.75x frequencies are identical at every step to 28 C. This is shown as a finding below. Lobster 020223 (marked "Not used") is in no fit.

# Crash temperatures: the rhythm crash of the crab tables (second neuron to crash, the Methods'
# definition) against the Prism crash-temperature file the paper's species comparisons used.
pc = {k: v["table"] for k, v in pr_crash.items()}
for key, sal in (("1x", 1.0), ("0.75x", 0.75), ("1.25x", 1.25)):
    t = pc[key]
    cancer = t[0].dropna().values
    homarus = t[1].dropna().values
    mine = crab_u[crab_u.salinity == sal].rhythm.dropna().values
    same = len(mine) == len(cancer) and np.allclose(np.sort(mine), np.sort(cancer))
    print(f"{key}: Prism Cancer n={len(cancer)} (mean {cancer.mean():.2f}); crab table rhythm crash n={len(mine)} "
          f"(mean {mine.mean():.2f}); same values: {same}; Prism Homarus n={len(homarus)} (mean {homarus.mean():.2f}, "
          f"range {homarus.min()} to {homarus.max()})")
print("\nCrab ramps with fewer than two neuron crashes (no rhythm crash):")
print(crab_u[crab_u.rhythm.isna()][["set", "salinity", "prep", "LP", "PY", "PD"]].to_string(index=False))
# Lobster: the step marked 'Crash' in Sheet4 against the Prism crash temperatures (unlabelled).
for sal, key in ((1.0, "1x"), (0.75, "0.75x"), (1.25, "1.25x")):
    r = lob_r[(lob_r.salinity == sal) & ~lob_r.not_used]
    print(f"Lobster {key}: Sheet4 crash steps {sorted(r.crash_step.dropna().tolist())}; "
          f"ramps without a Crash mark {r.crash_step.isna().sum()}; Prism crash temperatures {sorted(pc[key][1].dropna().tolist())}")

The crab crash temperatures in the Prism file are the second-neuron crash of the crab unit table, value for value, so the rhythm crash follows the Methods' definition. Crab 963_109 has no crash temperature at either salinity, so 1x has 20 crab values; the paper gives n = 21 for Fig. 7E. The lobster Prism values carry no preparation labels and are given to 0.1 C, finer than the 2 C steps of Sheet4, so they cannot be tied to a ramp; they are used as the paper's own values.

The two preparations' 0.75x ramps are different recordings (different sizes and checksums), but the burst table in the 111122 folder is the 120722 table, and the frequency table, the Prism fit data and the MATLAB file Lobster_Q10s_1x&075x.mat carry 120722's values under 111122 to 28 C. 111122's own 28 C burst file gives about 1.13 Hz, not 1.66 Hz. One 0.75x recording enters the lobster 0.75x fits twice and 111122's own 0.75x ramp is missing from them.

Neither record holds a script (MATLAB, Python, R or Spike2) among its files, in the lobster zip or in the first level of the other zips; the 21 inner crab zips were not opened. The paper says "All data and custom analysis scripts are freely available on the Zenodo repositories". Lobster 888_156 has frequencies in the table and no recording; 020223, marked "Not used", has none either.

def paired_report(a, b, label_a, label_b):
    ok = a.notna() & b.notna()
    a, b = a[ok], b[ok]
    t = stats.ttest_rel(a, b)
    print(f"n = {ok.sum()} paired; {label_a} {a.mean():.3f} +/- {a.std():.3f} Hz, {label_b} {b.mean():.3f} +/- {b.std():.3f} Hz; "
          f"difference {np.mean(b - a):+.3f} Hz; paired t = {t.statistic:.3f}, P = {t.pvalue:.3f}; "
          f"Shapiro-Wilk on differences P = {stats.shapiro(b - a).pvalue:.3f}")
    return a.mean(), b.mean(), t.pvalue

Result: reproduced (resting on an assumption). Nine of the ten counts match the paper directly: 14 of 20 PY and 15 of 20 PD crashes in 1x, 4 of 11 PD in 0.75x, 5 of 9 PY and 6 of 9 PD in 1.25x, and LP in 20 of 20, 11 of 11 and 9 of 9, PY in 11 of 11 in 0.75x. The first count depends on the reading of "all three neurons crashed at the same temperature". All three crashed in 9 of the 20 ramps, and in each of them the three crash temperatures lie within 1.0 C of each other, less than the 2 C step of the ramp (Methods). Counting those, reading ii (within one step) and reading iii (the same step reached) give 9 of 20, the paper's count; reading i (exactly equal recorded temperatures) gives 4. Reading ii is adopted: the criterion defines a neuron's crash as the step at which its bursts stop, so crashes within one step are crashes at the same step.

def neuron_mixed(g):
    long = g.melt(id_vars=["prep"], value_vars=["LP", "PY", "PD"], var_name="neuron", value_name="crash").dropna()
    m = smf.mixedlm("crash ~ C(neuron)", long, groups=long["prep"]).fit(reml=True)
    names = [n for n in m.params.index if n.startswith("C(neuron)")]
    wald = m.wald_test(" , ".join(f"{n} = 0" for n in names), scalar=True)
    chi2 = float(wald.statistic)
    k = len(names)
    n_obs, n_prep = len(long), long.prep.nunique()
    df2 = n_obs - n_prep - k
    return long, chi2, k, float(stats.chi2.sf(chi2, k)), float(stats.f.sf(chi2 / k, k, df2)), df2

rows = []
for sal, g in ((1.0, one_x), (0.75, s075u), (1.25, s125u)):
    long, chi2, k, p_chi2, p_f, df2 = neuron_mixed(g)
    means = long.groupby("neuron").crash.agg(["count", "mean", "std"]).round(2)
    print(f"{sal}x: neuron means\n{means.to_string()}")
    complete = g.dropna(subset=["LP", "PY", "PD"])
    fr = stats.friedmanchisquare(complete.LP, complete.PY, complete.PD) if len(complete) >= 3 else None
    rows.append({"salinity": sal, "obs": len(long), "preps": long.prep.nunique(), "Wald_chi2": round(chi2, 3),
                 "P_chi2": round(p_chi2, 3), f"P_F(k,resid)": round(p_f, 3), "df2": df2,
                 "complete_preps": len(complete), "Friedman_P": round(fr.pvalue, 3) if fr else np.nan})
fig2i_t = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(fig2i_t.to_string(index=False))

The paper used Prism's REML mixed-effects model with neuron as the repeated factor. Here a linear mixed model with a random intercept per preparation (statsmodels, REML) gives a Wald test of the neuron effect, without Prism's Geisser-Greenhouse correction; the Friedman test on preparations with all three crashes is shown as a variant.

Result: reproduced. No salinity shows a difference between the neurons' crash temperatures: the Wald test gives P = 0.322 (1x), 0.069 (0.75x) and 0.202 (1.25x) on the chi-square scale and 0.336, 0.106 and 0.254 on the F scale (paper 0.27, 0.12, 0.27); the Friedman variant gives 0.449 (1x) and 0.368 (0.75x), with too few complete preparations in 1.25x. The neuron means differ by at most 3 C (0.75x: PD 27.05 C, n = 4, against LP 30.05 C), and the crash order varies between ramps.

def q10_compare(groups, label):
    out = {}
    for rd in ("Q-a", "Q-b"):
        r = stns.shared_slope_test(groups, rd)
        fits = "; ".join(f"{g}: Q10 {f['q10']:.3f} [{f['q10_lo']:.2f}, {f['q10_hi']:.2f}], n = {f['n']}" for g, f in r["fits"].items())
        print(f"{label} {rd}: {fits}; F({r['df1']},{r['df2']}) = {r['F']:.3f}, P = {r['p']:.4f}, points {r['n_points']}")
        out[rd] = r
    return out

def tf(df, lo, hi):
    d = df[(df.temp >= lo) & (df.temp <= hi)]
    return d.temp.values, d.freq.values

c075 = crab_f[crab_f.set == "0.75x"]
fig2g = q10_compare({"1x": tf(c075[c075.salinity == 1.0], 10, 24), "0.75x": tf(c075[c075.salinity == 0.75], 10, 24)},
                    "Crab 0.75x set, 10-24 C")
print("Preparations:", c075.prep.nunique())

Crab mixed-effects model (Fig. 2F legend)¶

In [24]:
def mixed_model(d, sal_factor=False, log=False, label=""):
    d = d.copy()
    d["y"] = np.log10(d.freq) if log else d.freq
    sal = "C(salinity)" if sal_factor else "salinity"
    form = f"y ~ temp * {sal}"
    fits = {}
    for re_name, re_f in (("intercept", "1"), ("temp", "~temp"), ("salinity", "~salinity"), ("temp+salinity", "~temp+salinity")):
        try:
            m = smf.mixedlm(form, d, groups=d["prep"], re_formula=None if re_f == "1" else re_f).fit(reml=False, method=["lbfgs", "powell"])
            fits[re_name] = (m.aic if np.isfinite(m.aic) else np.inf, m.bic if np.isfinite(m.bic) else np.inf, m.converged)
        except Exception as e:
            fits[re_name] = (np.inf, np.inf, False)
    failed = [k for k, v in fits.items() if not np.isfinite(v[0])]
    best = min(fits, key=lambda k: (fits[k][0], fits[k][1]))
    re_f = {"intercept": None, "temp": "~temp", "salinity": "~salinity", "temp+salinity": "~temp+salinity"}[best]
    m = smf.mixedlm(form, d, groups=d["prep"], re_formula=re_f).fit(reml=True, method=["lbfgs", "powell"])
    fe = m.fe_params.index   # fixed effects only (m.params also holds the random-effect variances)
    terms = {"temperature": [n for n in fe if n == "temp"],
             "salinity": [n for n in fe if n.startswith(sal) and ":" not in n],
             "interaction": [n for n in fe if ":" in n]}
    res = {}
    for t, names in terms.items():
        w = m.wald_test(" , ".join(f"{n} = 0" for n in names), scalar=True)
        res[t] = float(w.pvalue)
    print(f"{label}: n = {len(d)} points, {d.prep.nunique()} preparations; random effects by AIC/BIC: {best} "
          f"(AIC/BIC {', '.join(f'{k} {v[0]:.1f}/{v[1]:.1f}' for k, v in fits.items())}); "
          f"P temperature {res['temperature']:.2g}, salinity {res['salinity']:.2g} ({len(terms['salinity'])} df), "
          f"interaction {res['interaction']:.2g}; candidates whose ML fit failed (left out): {failed or 'none'}")
    return res

The paper fitted lme4 in R and tested terms with lmerTest's F tests (Satterthwaite degrees of freedom). R is not available in this environment; the model here is statsmodels' linear mixed model (REML, random intercept per preparation, random slopes chosen by AIC then BIC among the same candidates), with Wald tests of each fixed-effect term. Wald tests are anti-conservative next to Satterthwaite F tests with few denominator df: a Wald P above 0.05 would stay above it, and a Wald P far below 0.05 would stay below. The Bayes factor comparison is not repeated. A candidate whose maximum-likelihood fit statsmodels could not evaluate (non-finite likelihood; the intercept-only model, mostly) is listed as failed and left out of the choice. Salinity as a factor (S-c, three salinities) has 2 df, where the criterion asks for 1; salinity as a number has 1. (The first run of this notebook tested salinity jointly with the variance of its random slope where the model had one; the tests here use the fixed effects only.)

Result: reproduced. Under S-c with frequency as the response and salinity as a number (one df, all 21 preparations), temperature (P = 1.5e-19) and the interaction (P = 0.0004) are significant and salinity is not (P = 0.16; paper 0.17), the paper's pattern. The other readings give two of the three parts, except S-a with log frequency (one): under S-b, the 0.75x set of n = 11 that the paper's n fits, temperature (P = 1.5e-15) and the interaction (P = 0.0006) are significant, but so is salinity (P = 0.022 with frequency, 0.020 with log frequency); under S-a with frequency, temperature is significant and salinity is not, but the interaction is not (P = 0.28). The reading that gives the pattern is not the one whose n matches the paper's.

def at10(df, sal=1.0, exclude=()):
    d = df[(df.salinity == sal) & (df.temp == 10) & ~df.prep.isin(exclude)]
    return d.groupby("prep").freq.first()

crab10 = at10(crab_f)
lob10 = at10(lob_f, exclude=lob_r[lob_r.not_used].prep.tolist())
w = stats.ttest_ind(crab10, lob10, equal_var=False)
print(f"R-a: crab n = {len(crab10)}, {crab10.mean():.3f} +/- {crab10.std():.3f} Hz; lobster n = {len(lob10)}, "
      f"{lob10.mean():.3f} +/- {lob10.std():.3f} Hz; Welch t = {w.statistic:.2f}, P = {w.pvalue:.2g}")
crab_base = crab_s[crab_s.salinity == 1.0].groupby("prep").freq.first().dropna()
w2 = stats.ttest_ind(crab_base, lob10, equal_var=False)

      f"no lobster salinity series is deposited, so the lobster side stays the 10 C ramp step: Welch P = {w2.pvalue:.2g}")

Result: partially reproduced. Temperature and the temperature by salinity interaction are significant under every reading over all deposited ramps (temperature P from 1e-07 to 2e-06, interaction P from 0.0003 to 0.014), but salinity alone is not (P from 0.26 to 0.79), where the paper found P = 0.001. Over the ramps Sheet4 marks with a Crash step (10, 13 and 8, close to the paper's n of 10, 14 and 8), temperature is significant under every reading (P from 1e-06 to 0.0002), the interaction under three of four (P from 0.002 to 0.026; 0.07 with frequency as the response and salinity as a factor), and salinity under none (P from 0.40 to 0.71). The variant without the 4.68 Hz value and the duplicated 0.75x ramp gives the same pattern (salinity P = 0.16 and 0.41). Two of the three terms are significant under 9 of the 10 readings; none gives all three.

def finite_sorted(a):
    a = np.asarray(a, float).ravel()
    return np.sort(a[np.isfinite(a)])

for sal, hi, mk, side in ((0.75, 24, "Lobster_Q10s_1x&075x.mat", "low"), (1.25, 22, "Lobster_Q10s_1x&125x.mat", "high")):

    pg = stns.prism_xy_groups(pr_freq[f"{sal}x"])[f"Homam {sal}x"].loc[10:hi]
    for lab, tab_vals, other in (("1x controls", d[(d.salinity == 1.0) & d.temp.between(10, hi)].freq,
                                  {"MATLAB norm": mats[mk]["norm"][:rows_hi]}),

            for k, b in ((k, finite_sorted(v)) for k, v in other.items())))

# Since the deposit gives no point to drop, each point is left out in turn (Q-a).
loo = {}
for sal, hi in ((0.75, 24), (1.25, 22)):
    preps, d = lob_set(sal)
    g = {"1x": tf(d[d.salinity == 1.0], 10, hi), f"{sal}x": tf(d[d.salinity == sal], 10, hi)}
    ps = []
    for name in g:
        T, F = g[name]
        for k in range(len(T)):
            gg = dict(g)
            gg[name] = (np.delete(T, k), np.delete(F, k))
            ps.append(stns.shared_slope_test(gg, "Q-a")["p"])
    loo[sal] = np.array(ps)
    print(f"{sal}x set, each of {len(ps)} points left out in turn (Q-a): P from {loo[sal].min():.4f} to {loo[sal].max():.4f}, "
          f"median {np.median(loo[sal]):.4f}; P > 0.05 in {int((loo[sal] > 0.05).sum())} of {len(ps)}")

Result: not reproduced. The four Q10s are within tolerance under Q-a (1x controls 1.587 and 0.75x 1.859 in the 0.75x set, paper 1.61 and 1.85; 1x controls 1.795 and 1.25x 1.485 in the 1.25x set, paper 1.87 and 1.48), and the 1.25x set shows no difference (P = 0.098; paper 0.055). But in the 0.75x set the slopes differ: F(1,210) = 4.04, P = 0.046 under Q-a and P = 0.041 under Q-b (paper F(1,209) = 3.495, P = 0.063). The deposited data give one point more than the paper in each set (214 and 176 against 213 and 175), and the authors' MATLAB files and Prism sheets hold the same values as the tables, point for point, so the deposit does not show which point the paper left out. Left out in turn, the 214 points of the 0.75x set give P from 0.019 to 0.107 (above 0.05 for 60 of them); the 176 of the 1.25x set give P from 0.038 to 0.205 (above 0.05 for 175). The miss is marginal and depends on which point the paper dropped. Without the duplicated 111122 0.75x ramp, P = 0.052 under Q-a and 0.044 under Q-b.

In vivo PPG recordings (Fig. 8)¶

Each exposure is a zip of 2-min ABF files (5 kHz, one channel) inside one of four zips of record 17794764. Every exposure is read, each file is decimated to 50 Hz, the files are joined in the order of their start times, and a spectrogram over 0 to 3 Hz is made with 10-s windows and 50% overlap (the claims file's standard choices). The claims file's rule gives a window a rhythm when its peak power between 0.3 and 3 Hz is above three times the window's median power (reading B-a over the hour, B-b over the first 30 min). As a reference the same rule is applied to the same trace with its samples shuffled (a flat spectrum), under the claim's seed and four more. Three variants calibrated on the shuffled trace are this attempt's: the per-window peak ratio above the 99th percentile of the shuffled trace's; and on the mean spectrum of each 1-min block (12 windows), the peak ratio, or the prominence of the largest local peak between 0.4 and 2.8 Hz over the power 0.3 to 0.5 Hz on either side, above the shuffled trace's 99th percentile. An exposure keeps its rhythm under a rule when at least half its windows or blocks have a band. The reads run in eight threads; the time they took is printed below.

In [35]:
import hashlib
import zlib
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

seed = zlib.crc32(b"carrier-2026/fig8-invivo-rhythm-maintained")
seeds = [seed + d for d in (0, 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000)]
jobs = [(k, n) for k in stns.INVIVO_ZIPS for n, _ in nested[k] if n.endswith(".zip")]
t0 = time.time()
with ThreadPoolExecutor(8) as ex:
    iv = list(ex.map(lambda j: stns.process_exposure(j[0], j[1], seeds), jobs))
print(f"{len(iv)} exposures read and analysed in {(time.time() - t0) / 60:.1f} min")
ivt = pd.DataFrame([{k: v for k, v in r.items() if k not in ("spectrogram", "file_md5", "peak_hz")} for r in iv])
ivt["null_mean"] = ivt.null_frac_present.apply(np.mean)
ivt["null_max"] = ivt.null_frac_present.apply(np.max)
for v in ("cal", "avg", "prom"):
    for sfx in ("", "_first30"):
        ivt[f"{v}{sfx}_seed0"] = ivt[v + sfx].apply(lambda x: x[0])
        ivt[f"{v}{sfx}_min5"] = ivt[v + sfx].apply(min)
        ivt[f"{v}{sfx}_max5"] = ivt[v + sfx].apply(max)
ivt["fingerprint"] = [hashlib.md5("".join(r["file_md5"]).encode()).hexdigest()[:12] for r in iv]

Several in vivo exposures are the same recording filed under two names: their ABF files are identical, file for file. The list above gives each pair. A pair filed under two animals at one salinity counts one animal twice; the crab pair is filed under two salinities of one animal.

Every exposure labelled "1Hour" holds 16 two-minute files, about 32 min of recording, and the one labelled "15Hours" holds the same 32 min. The paper describes 1-h exposures (and 2.5-h and 15-h ones); the second half of each hour is not in the deposit.

rules = {"claims file rule (ratio 3)": ("frac_present", "frac_present_first30"),

         "calibrated, 1-min prominence": ("prom_seed0", "prom_first30_seed0")}
summ = []
for name, (whole, first30) in rules.items():
    for span, c in (("whole recording", whole), ("first 30 min (B-b)", first30)):
        keep = one_h[c] >= 0.5
        lost = one_h[~keep]
        row = {"rule": name, "span": span, "keep, of 58": int(keep.sum()),
               "keep, distinct recordings": int(one_h[keep].fingerprint.nunique()),
               "crab keep": int(keep[one_h.species == "Crab"].sum()), "lobster keep": int(keep[one_h.species == "Lobster"].sum()),
               "below half": ", ".join(f"{r.species[0]}{r.animal} {r.salinity}x" for r in lost.itertuples())}
        summ.append(row)
summ = pd.DataFrame(summ)

# Every 1-h spectrogram (the criterion asks for all), power over 0 to 3 Hz relative to each
# window's median (dB, colour limits -5 to 20 dB), and below it the peak frequency between 0.3 and
# 3 Hz in each 10-s window. Titles give the fraction of windows over the first 30 min that keep a
# band under the four rules (claims file rule; calibrated per window, 1-min ratio, 1-min prominence).
one_iv = sorted([r for r in iv if r["hours"] == 1], key=lambda r: (r["species"], r["salinity"], r["animal"]))
key = {(r.species, r.salinity, r.animal): r for r in one_h.itertuples()}
ncol = 6
for sp in ("Crab", "Lobster"):
    rs = [r for r in one_iv if r["species"] == sp]
    nrow = int(np.ceil(len(rs) / ncol))
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2 * nrow, ncol, figsize=(18, 3.2 * nrow), sharex=True,
                             gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [3, 1] * nrow})
    for k, r in enumerate(rs):
        ax, axp = axes[2 * (k // ncol), k % ncol], axes[2 * (k // ncol) + 1, k % ncol]
        fr, tt, S = r["spectrogram"]
        ax.pcolormesh(tt / 60, fr, 10 * np.log10(S / np.median(S, axis=0)), shading="auto", vmin=-5, vmax=20)
        q = key[(sp, r["salinity"], r["animal"])]
        ax.set_title(f"{sp} {r['animal']} {r['salinity']}x: {q.frac_present_first30:.2f}/{q.cal_first30_seed0:.2f}/"
                     f"{q.avg_first30_seed0:.2f}/{q.prom_first30_seed0:.2f}", fontsize=8)
        axp.plot(tt / 60, r["peak_hz"], ".", ms=1)
        axp.set_ylim(0, 3)
    for k in range(len(rs), nrow * ncol):
        axes[2 * (k // ncol), k % ncol].axis("off")
        axes[2 * (k // ncol) + 1, k % ncol].axis("off")
    fig.suptitle(f"{sp}, every 1-h exposure: spectrogram (Hz against min) and peak frequency per window", y=1.0)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
print("Power range plotted (dB re window median): every value is clipped to -5 to 20 dB;",
      "share of cells above 20 dB:", round(float(np.mean([np.mean(10 * np.log10(r["spectrogram"][2] / np.median(r["spectrogram"][2], axis=0)) > 20) for r in one_iv])), 4))

# Crab 18: a peak at 2.3 to 2.4 Hz at 0.25x and 0.5x. Is it a harmonic of a band at half the
# frequency, as at 0.75x (bands at 1.3 and 2.6 Hz)? Power at the peak and at half its frequency,
# relative to the window median, medians over windows.
for sal in (0.25, 0.5, 0.75):
    r = next(x for x in one_iv if x["species"] == "Crab" and x["animal"] == 18 and x["salinity"] == sal)
    fr, tt, S = r["spectrogram"]
    rel = S / np.median(S, axis=0)
    pk = float(np.median(r["peak_hz"]))
    j, jh, j2 = int(np.argmin(abs(fr - pk))), int(np.argmin(abs(fr - pk / 2))), int(np.argmin(abs(fr - 2 * pk)))
    print(f"Crab 18 {sal}x: median peak {pk:.2f} Hz, peak frequency within 0.1 Hz of it in "
          f"{np.mean(abs(r['peak_hz'] - pk) <= 0.1):.2f} of windows; median power at {fr[j]:.1f} Hz {np.median(rel[j]):.1f}x "
          f"at {fr[jh]:.1f} Hz {np.median(rel[jh]):.1f}x and at {fr[j2]:.1f} Hz {np.median(rel[j2]):.1f}x the window median")

Result: blocked (methods underspecified). The claims file's rule (peak above three times the median) finds a band in 0.978 to 1.000 of the windows of every 1-h exposure, over the recording and over the first 30 min (B-b), but it cannot show a crash: the same traces with their samples shuffled pass it in 0.901 to 0.992 of their windows. Rules calibrated on the shuffled traces disagree on the crab exposures. Over the first 30 min, 53 of 58 exposures keep a band in at least half the windows under the per-window calibrated ratio (51 to 53 over the five seeds; below half: crab 18 at 0.25x and 0.5x, crab 10 at 0.25x and 0.5x, crab 12 at 1.25x), 58 of 58 under the 1-min mean ratio, and 46 of 58 under the 1-min prominence (46 to 52 over the seeds; twelve crab exposures below half). Every lobster exposure keeps its band under all four rules. The spectrograms show sharp, steady bands in most lobster and some crab exposures, and broad or faint ones in several crab exposures; crab 18 at 0.25x has a narrow line at 2.4 Hz in 0.81 of its windows and nothing at 1.2 Hz, while at 0.75x its band is at 1.3 Hz with a harmonic at 2.6 Hz. The paper judged the spectrograms by eye and gives no rule, so whether a faint crab band is a rhythm cannot be settled here. Each "1-h" exposure holds 30 to 32 min, so B-a, over the hour, cannot be applied as written. The 58 exposures are 51 distinct recordings (7 crab and 5 lobster animals with decreased salinity, 7 crab and 4 lobster with increased; paper 6, 5, 6 and 5).

Blocked claims¶

  • fig1e-cb-salinity-crash-fractions: the crab salinity table holds 1x, 0.75x, 1.25x and 1.5x only. The three counts it gives match the paper (fig1e cell above), but the criterion needs all five salinities, or four for a partial result. Whether each preparation crashed in 0.5x and 1.75x is only in the raw ABF recordings, inside 21 nested zips of 1.1 to 2.1 GB each (37 GB), which hold the salinity-series preparations (first entries above) in files named by sequence number only. Reading them at the rate printed above, mapping each file to a salinity without a protocol log, and detecting bursts without the paper's criteria does not fit the run.
  • fig4b, fig4d, fig4e: the lobster salinity series are in neither record (finding above; the lobster zip's Excel and text files are all ramp burst tables).
  • fig5b-ha-lp-crashes-before-py, and fig6a and fig6b, which depend on it: the deposited tables give the lobster rhythm crash only; the LP and PY crash temperatures of each lobster ramp are not tabulated (the lobster 1x saline sheet holds frequencies, the MATLAB files frequencies and Q10s). LP and PY burst files exist for 8 of the 19 preparations (six "For Analysis" folders and two "1X TEXT FILES" folders, counted below), fewer than the paper's n of 12 to 18; the rest would need LP and PY identified in 33 GB of Spike2 recordings, with burst criteria the paper does not give.
  • fig8-invivo-rhythm-maintained: tested above; blocked because no rule with a basis in the paper decides whether the faint crab bands are a rhythm, and the deposit holds 32 min of each hour.
  • fig9-15h-mortality: the deposit holds one 15-h recording (Lobster 9, 0.25x, 32 min of it) and no record of which animals survived.

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. The isolated-STNS claims use the authors' own per-preparation values from the deposited tables; the burst detection on the raw recordings is not repeated. The Q10 fits reproduce the deposited Prism outputs to every printed digit under the semi-log model (Q-a). The mixed models are statsmodels' linear mixed models with Wald tests, not lme4 with lmerTest's Satterthwaite F tests, and Prism's REML repeated-measures model is replaced by a mixed model with a random intercept per preparation, without the Geisser-Greenhouse correction. The in vivo rhythm is judged by the claims file's band rule and three rules calibrated on shuffled traces, not by eye; they disagree on the crab exposures, and the claim is left blocked.

What was found about the datasets. The deposit holds the authors' analysis tables and Prism files, which reproduce exactly the paper's Q10 statistics of Figs. 2G, 2H, 3B and 7A to 7C; those of Fig. 5D and of the PY-on phase (Fig. 3C) differ. In them, lobster 111122's 0.75x ramp is a copy of 120722's (the 111122 recording itself is deposited and differs); one crab 1.25x crash temperature is 36 C in the Prism file and 26 C in the unit table, the source of the paper's two crab 1.25x means; and one lobster 1x value is 4.68 Hz. In the in vivo data, seven exposures are the same recordings as seven others under another animal or salinity, and each "1-h" exposure holds 32 min. The lobster salinity series, the lobster neuron crash temperatures, the raw recording of lobster 888_156 and the 15-h survival records are not in either record, and no analysis script, which the paper says is deposited, was found in the files read (the 21 inner crab zips were read only at their start). The deposited Prism sheets and MATLAB files hold the same lobster frequencies as the tables, so the one extra point per Fig. 5D set cannot be traced. The crab tables label 10 C with a date, list 888_136 as two preparations and leave 888_145 out of the Animals sheet.
